tagline: Old shore towns, stitched together by water.
intro: From Berlin's rows of nineteenth-century commercial buildings, the drive reaches Snow Hill and continues toward Pocomoke City. Snow Hill stands at the head of navigation on the Pocomoke River and was made a port of entry in 1694. Its settlers may have named it for a street in London, though the town sits 16 feet above sea level and seldom sees snow.
The Blue Crab name once covered two routes, now the Lower Eastern Shore section of Chesapeake Country and the Cape to Cape byway, which runs through Berlin and Snow Hill.

moments.title: Berlin Commercial District
moments.text: About 47 small commercial buildings of the late nineteenth century line both sides of the main street, most of them built in rows with shared walls.

moments.title: All Hallows Episcopal Church
moments.text: A 1748 tax on tobacco paid for this church, finished in 1756 and unusually elaborate for its time and place; it is still an active parish.

moments.title: Julia A. Purnell Museum
moments.text: The 1891 St. Agnes Catholic Church now holds Julia Purnell's needlework of Snow Hill houses and gardens, made in her eighties and nineties, along with her son's miniature fleas.
